video_title: The Counterintuitive Story of the Hormuz Oil Crisis with Rory Johnston | TGS 240
gist: Recorded October 22, Commodity Context's Rory Johnston updates Nate Hagens on the eighth month of the Iran war: non-Iranian Gulf crude exports briefly recovered to pre-war levels in late September before Iran's heaviest attacks of the war, but freight is $20-30/bbl (10x normal), more than 2 billion barrels of Middle East output has been lost, and refined products, especially diesel (cracks around 5-6x normal, New York Harbor diesel futures at $227/bbl), are the real crisis. He explains China's mysterious 5.5 mb/d import collapse ('Beijing swing'), the record WTI-Brent dislocation, Russia's diesel export collapse, OPEC strains after the UAE's exit, and base/best/worst cases for 2027.

themes.theme: Hormuz flows, freight and a balkanized market

insights.claim: Non-Iranian crude exports through Hormuz briefly recovered to pre-war levels through late September, but Iran then re-escalated to its heaviest attacks of the war (about two attacks a day, starting after the UN General Assembly ended), pulling volumes back.
insights.speaker: Rory Johnston
insights.so_what: Headline 'recovery' narratives are fragile; flows can reverse quickly with attack intensity.

insights.claim: Shipping a barrel from the Persian Gulf to Asia now costs about $20-30 versus a normal $2-3, driven by war-risk insurance and a dark-transit system of ship-to-ship transfers.
insights.speaker: Rory Johnston
insights.so_what: Tanker owners and commodity traders capture extraordinary margins while exporters bear the cost.
insights.quote: Normally it costs like two to three bucks to ship a barrel from the Persian Gulf to Northeast Asia. Now that's 10X that volume.

insights.claim: The accumulated loss of Middle East oil output versus expectations this year exceeds two billion barrels, by far the largest supply shock in the history of the market, partly absorbed by a pre-war surplus.
insights.speaker: Rory Johnston
insights.so_what: Inventories have been drained, so even small ongoing deficits now carry more price risk than large ones did in March.
insights.quote: the loss is over two billion barrels.

insights.claim: Johnston argues that because stocks have been drawn down so heavily, a smaller daily deficit today is as concerning or more so than the large deficit with high inventories in March.
insights.speaker: Rory Johnston
insights.so_what: Stock-and-flow framing: watch inventories, not just daily flow deficits, for price direction.

insights.claim: High freight costs have fragmented the oil market: the US Gulf Coast WTI versus Dated Brent spread blew out to a record of more than $40 a barrel in early October, wider than on April 20, 2020 when WTI traded at negative $37, while North Sea physical premiums hit all-time highs and West African discounts record lows.
insights.speaker: Rory Johnston
insights.so_what: Exporting regions (US Gulf, West Africa) face deep discounts while importing regions pay record premiums, creating large arbitrage for those with shipping.
insights.quote: we find ourselves kind of now trapped in this horrific balkanized oil market

insights.claim: Iraq recovered fastest by offering discounts of about $37 a barrel (roughly a third of the headline price) for Basra loadings in September and by trucking 100,000-200,000 bpd west through Syria to the Mediterranean.
insights.speaker: Rory Johnston
insights.so_what: Commodity traders like Trafigura, Vitol and Glencore enjoy margins far above their usual cents per barrel.

insights.claim: The crude recovery is crude-only because rerouting pipelines (Saudi East-West to the Red Sea and the UAE's ADCOP to the Gulf of Oman) carry only crude; refined product exports remain below half of pre-war levels and LNG remains well below pre-war, with about 20% of Qatar's Ras Laffan capacity damaged and likely offline for years.
insights.speaker: Rory Johnston
insights.so_what: Product and LNG tightness will outlast crude normalisation, supporting refining and LNG margins elsewhere.
insights.quote: Refined products still less than half, um, of their pre-war levels.

insights.claim: Pre-war, 20-21 million barrels a day of total petroleum left Hormuz, about 15 million crude and 5 million refined products.
insights.speaker: Rory Johnston
insights.so_what: Baseline for judging the scale of ongoing losses.

insights.claim: If the war ended, Johnston expects insurance premiums to fall quickly but not to pre-war levels, and the tanker tie-up from dark shuttle trades to heal over a couple of months.
insights.speaker: Rory Johnston
insights.so_what: Tanker rates would normalise faster than war-risk insurance pricing.

insights.claim: New York Harbor diesel futures hit about $227 a barrel in late September, the highest in history, with the diesel crack spread around $120 versus a long-term norm of about $20, roughly 5-6x normal.
insights.speaker: Rory Johnston
insights.so_what: Refiners are earning record margins; diesel-intensive sectors (trucking, farming, mining) face cost shocks.

insights.claim: Johnston's earlier call for $150-200 oil did not materialise in crude but effectively did in diesel, because demand destruction is driven by refined products, and an unmitigated Hormuz shock required destroying about 6-8 million bpd of demand when $120-130 oil historically only destroyed 1-2 million.
insights.speaker: Rory Johnston
insights.so_what: Price rationing is happening through product cracks rather than the crude benchmark.
insights.quote: it's not crude oil that drives demand destruction, it's the refined products

insights.claim: The market has lost roughly 1-1.5 million bpd of diesel supply out of a 25-30 million bpd global market, equivalent in scale to a 5-million-plus bpd deficit in total oil; Johnston attributes it roughly 60/40 to the Iran war versus Ukraine's attacks on Russian refineries.
insights.speaker: Rory Johnston
insights.so_what: Diesel tightness has two independent geopolitical drivers, making relief slower.

insights.claim: Middle East diesel exports are down about 750,000 to 1 million bpd due to crude-prioritised logistics (VLCC economics), Iranian strikes on Saudi, UAE and Kuwaiti refineries, and escalating Houthi attacks on Saudi Red Sea coast refineries.
insights.speaker: Rory Johnston
insights.so_what: Gulf product export capacity is structurally impaired, not just logistically blocked.

insights.claim: Russian diesel exports, normally about 900,000 bpd (second only to the US at 1.1-1.2 million), fell to barely over 100,000 bpd after Ukrainian strikes took up to half of Russia's refinery fleet offline and Moscow banned gasoline, jet and then diesel exports.
insights.speaker: Rory Johnston
insights.so_what: US product exporters gain pricing power in global diesel.

insights.claim: Johnston calls Trump's announced diesel deal with Putin a 'nothing burger': Putin pledged 500,000 tons of diesel in November, only about 125,000 bpd (roughly current Russian exports and a tenth of normal), in exchange for six months of sanctions relief on Russian diesel through April 7.
insights.speaker: Rory Johnston
insights.so_what: The deal will not materially ease diesel prices; the Kremlin gained most.

insights.claim: US refineries are deferring maintenance because record margins mean an extra month of running can earn almost a year's profit, raising the probability of unplanned outages in a fragile market.
insights.speaker: Rory Johnston
insights.so_what: Elevated outage risk heading into winter could trigger product price spikes.
insights.quote: you could make almost a year's worth of profit off of that one month of refining.

insights.claim: US commercial petroleum stocks fell more than 13 million barrels in a week when they normally build, and crude, gasoline and diesel are all below their five-year lows for the season; jet fuel is the exception after refiners shifted yields about 1% toward jet.
insights.speaker: Rory Johnston
insights.so_what: Heating-fuel inventories enter winter crucially low; a warm Super El Niño winter may be the main relief.

insights.claim: Johnston does not expect outright physical shortages in North America, Europe or wealthy Asia absent government trade interference, but poorer emerging markets such as Sri Lanka and Indonesia are being priced out, and India has seen LPG shortages push households back to wood, coal and dung.
insights.speaker: Rory Johnston
insights.so_what: Demand destruction is concentrated in the poorest importers, a source of EM macro and humanitarian stress.
insights.quote: the unfortunate reality of global capitalist trade is that it will be born by the poorest members of society.

insights.claim: China cut crude imports by about 5.5 million bpd between the December-February pre-war average and the June-July bottom, about 45% of pre-war imports, while the rest of Asia's imports rebounded to and above pre-war levels after May.
insights.speaker: Rory Johnston
insights.so_what: China's restraint was the single biggest shock absorber for the market and its reversal is a key upside price risk.
insights.quote: China cut crude oil imports by about five and a half million barrels a day.

insights.claim: About half of China's import cut came from lower refinery runs after Beijing capped domestic product prices (diesel up only 30% while global wholesale diesel doubled), collapsing refining margins to record lows; the rest likely came from pre-war stockbuilding of 0.5-1 million bpd and probable undisclosed crude and product SPR releases.
insights.speaker: Rory Johnston
insights.so_what: If China's stockbuild was large, it may not need to restore imports fully, which is bearish for oil.

insights.claim: China's apparent diesel demand fell about 20% year over year this summer while road freight (about 70% of Chinese diesel use) rose 3.5%, a gap Johnston says is unexplainable without undisclosed strategic product releases, even allowing for LNG and electric trucking.
insights.speaker: Rory Johnston
insights.so_what: Chinese strategic product stocks are likely being drawn and will need rebuilding.

insights.claim: Johnston theorises China absorbed the shock beyond its own needs to backstop its key export markets in Asia and Europe, since real estate can no longer reflate its economy and Trump's second-term trade war is pushing it to diversify away from the US.
insights.speaker: Rory Johnston
insights.so_what: Chinese energy policy is now an instrument for protecting export demand.

insights.claim: Johnston and Nate Hagens expect energy data to get more opaque as energy becomes a national security matter, noting the EIA has cancelled many critical surveys and been aggressively defunded under Trump 2, with the early 2010s as the high-water mark of government data transparency.
insights.speaker: Rory Johnston / Nate Hagens
insights.so_what: Alternative data such as tanker tracking (e.g., Kepler) gains value, but cannot replace government surveys.

themes.theme: Why prices stayed contained and the macro backdrop

insights.claim: Johnston's three big surprises are China's import collapse, the cushion from entering the year with a large surplus and an expected post-war glut, and Trump's jawboning injecting upside volatility; never before was the oil market as prepared for such a shock.
insights.speaker: Rory Johnston
insights.so_what: The calm in crude is conditional on these buffers, which are depleting.
insights.quote: Never before in history was the oil market as prepared, as kind of steeled for this moment as now.

insights.claim: Global economies have proven more resilient to high oil prices than expected, partly because the S&P 500 is now effectively an AI index insulated from old-economy pressures, though tech investors are most exposed to war-driven inflation and higher rates.
insights.speaker: Rory Johnston
insights.so_what: Persistent energy inflation is a key risk to cheap-debt-funded AI data center build-outs.
insights.quote: is primarily now an AI index in terms of its actual gain.

insights.claim: Before the war Johnston expected Brent to fall to $50 or below in 2026 to force supply rationalisation; that surplus has been erased, so a 2027 surplus would first need to rebuild inventories, delaying downward pressure.
insights.speaker: Rory Johnston
insights.so_what: Lower prices are deferred rather than cancelled; 2028 is the likely rationalisation year in a peace scenario.

insights.claim: US crude production, expected by the EIA to contract this year at $40-60 oil, is instead still rising to fresh all-time monthly highs, though not a 'drill, baby, drill' surge; Johnston says the era of 1 million-plus bpd annual growth at $65 crude is over.
insights.speaker: Rory Johnston
insights.so_what: Shale responds to triple-digit prices but would plateau and decline near $50.
insights.quote: the days of, you know, a million barrels a day plus of US crude production growth with crude at $65 a barrel, those are behind us.

insights.claim: Nate Hagens argues a credit-driven affordability collapse makes a 2009- or 2020-style price crash (even negative prices) at least as likely as a super spike, and Johnston agrees nothing prevents oil going negative if a quick peace leads into 2028 with full restocking, absent Saudi cuts or Chinese SPR buying.
insights.speaker: Nate Hagens / Rory Johnston
insights.so_what: Tail risk is two-sided; long-dated hedges should account for crash scenarios.

insights.claim: The belly of oil futures curves has begun rising notably as participants hedge the status quo into 2027 and 2028, a bullish sign that the market no longer assumes a quick return to surplus.
insights.speaker: Rory Johnston
insights.so_what: Deferred contracts are re-pricing geopolitical risk premium.

insights.claim: Iranian crude production is near its lowest since the 1980s and exports are almost nil under the US blockade, down from about 2 million bpd of exports (on roughly 4 million bpd production) as recently as April; Johnston expects recovery to pre-war levels within a couple of months if the blockade lifts.
insights.speaker: Rory Johnston
insights.so_what: About 2 million bpd of Iranian supply is a quick-return bearish swing factor in any settlement.

insights.claim: An economist returning from Tehran reported 100%-plus annualised inflation from rial depreciation but no hyperinflation behaviour or major goods shortages, as Iran has turned autarkic and wealthy Iranians' trapped spending recycles domestically.
insights.speaker: Rory Johnston
insights.so_what: Washington's 'siege chicken' bet that the blockade bankrupts Tehran quickly may be overstated.

insights.claim: The UAE's exit from OPEC earlier this year, now pumping full out, is the largest loss in the group's history because of its spare capacity; Saudi Arabia has turned more price-hawkish while Iraq wants to produce flat out, and if Iraq leaves 'OPEC is pretty dead'.
insights.speaker: Rory Johnston
insights.so_what: Expect more unilateral Saudi cuts in the new year and weaker OPEC cohesion.
insights.quote: if Iraq leaves, I think OPEC is pretty dead.

insights.claim: Johnston blames the pre-war glut fundamentally on OPEC's unsustainable 2022-2024 production cuts, whose unwinding created the surplus.
insights.speaker: Rory Johnston
insights.so_what: Post-war oversupply would be even larger as non-OPEC growth continued during the war.
insights.quote: I still think is fundamentally OPEC's fault

insights.claim: The UAE has been the war's most aggressive participant (joining attacks, pioneering the dark-transit system, reportedly paying Iran early on, and sourcing drone defense from Israel and Ukraine), while Saudi Arabia has stayed quiet; Gulf states are proposing about half a dozen new pipelines to route around Iran and are reducing dependence on the US security umbrella.
insights.speaker: Rory Johnston
insights.so_what: A post-Carter Doctrine Gulf means pipeline capex and weaker US leverage over producers.
insights.quote: that security umbrella didn't really get them much in terms of actual security when it really mattered.

insights.claim: Johnston says indications are that last month's East-West Pipeline outage was caused by Iranian proxies in southern Iraq rather than the Houthis, a more direct Iranian attack.
insights.speaker: Rory Johnston
insights.so_what: Saudi's main Hormuz bypass is vulnerable from multiple directions.

insights.claim: India and other importers are committing to larger strategic stockpiles, often in partnership with Gulf exporters such as ADNOC, which want forward-deployed barrels to keep selling if Hormuz is blocked again.
insights.speaker: Rory Johnston
insights.so_what: Structural restocking demand will support prices after the war.

insights.claim: Johnston's 2027 base case is that the conflict persists at least four to six more months with on-and-off Iranian attacks and extremely high shipping costs but some volumetric relief.
insights.speaker: Rory Johnston
insights.so_what: Expect continued elevated product prices and freight through early 2027.

insights.claim: His best case is that a midterm shellacking chastens Trump into ending the war, possibly with Iran receiving some payoff or shadow 'subscription' toll (as Kepler's Michele Brillhard personally believes), which would return the market to surplus with a year to rebuild stocks and lower prices in 2028.
insights.speaker: Rory Johnston
insights.so_what: Even a $1 billion monthly payoff to Tehran is far cheaper than the economic cost of the current status quo.
insights.quote: even a billion dollars a month being paid to Tehran is an order of magnitude cheaper than the implications of a continuation of this current scenario.

insights.claim: In the worst case, the conflict continues at current levels for six more months, inventories keep falling and crude and products head higher until demand throttles back, with possible nonlinear jumps on events like another East-West Pipeline outage.
insights.speaker: Rory Johnston
insights.so_what: The market could snap back to historical risk-pricing psychology, producing a sharp spike.

insights.claim: Johnston says a Democratic midterm sweep could either constrain the war through hearings and Pentagon defunding or provoke Trump to re-escalate with Israel for a rally-around-the-flag effect.
insights.speaker: Rory Johnston
insights.so_what: The midterms are a binary geopolitical catalyst for oil.
